s1.p1: [Closure](⟦f0⟧) is an effect that allows variables in the context of the parent function—which returns the function—to be ‘hidden’.
s1.p2: [Closure](⟦f1⟧) is a combination of a function and the lexical environment in which that function was declared.
s1.p3: If a function returns a function, the lexical environment of the parent function is included in the scope chain of the child function.
s1.p4: In other words, all arguments passed to the parent function upon invocation, as well as all variables and functions declared within it, will be accessible to the child function (it ‘sees’ them).
s1.p5: ^^However, they will not be accessible anywhere else, as references to them are only available to the child function.^^
s1.p6: So, the closure effect only occurs if a function returns a function.

s1.p36: The closure effect is often used to protect variables, but it is important to remember that this is merely a side effect, not a technique in its own right, and that this effect can lead to memory leaks.
s2.p1: Combining IIFE with the closure effect gives us one of the design patterns known as the ‘Module’ pattern, which, unfortunately, is widely used in development as well as when building applications.
s2.p2: Any application is built from modules, each of which has its own isolated scope.
s2.p3: All variables and functions declared within a module are accessible only within that module.
s2.p4: However, in order to ‘hide’ variables and functions within a module, it makes more sense to use currying rather than relying on the side effect of the garbage collector.
s2.p5: I recommend that you familiarise yourself thoroughly with currying, a technique borrowed from functional programming languages; it is a more correct way not only to ‘hide’ variables within a function (or module), but also to construct elegant chained computations.
